extracted.intended_audience: parties and practitioners in TTAB trademark inter partes proceedings (attorneys, representatives, and litigants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on disclosure, discovery scope, and expert-witness procedures in Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB) inter partes proceedings, including Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 requirements, timing, form, limits on ESI, and remedies for noncompliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert witness written report content
rubrics_metrics.description: The report must contain: (i) a complete statement of all opinions the witness will express and the basis and reasons for them; (ii) the facts or data considered by the witness in forming them; (iii) any exhibits that will be used to summarize or support them; (iv) the witness's qualifications, including a list of all publications authored in the previous 10 years; (v) a list of all other cases in which, during the previous 4 years, the witness testified as an expert at trial or by deposition; and (vi) a statement of the compensation to be paid for the study and testimony in the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tracks Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2)(B). Only retained experts are required to provide such a written report unless otherwise stipulated or ordered. The report enables adversary discovery about the expert's opinions and bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure for witnesses who do not provide a written report
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless otherwise stipulated or ordered, if the witness is not required to provide a written report, the disclosure must state: (i) the subject matter on which the witness is expected to present evidence under Federal Rule of Evidence 702, 703, or 705; and (ii) a summary of the facts and opinions to which the witness is expected to testify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This summarizes Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2)(C) and addresses unretained experts or witnesses whose testimony falls under expert-evidence rules but who do not produce a full report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of expert disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: A party must make expert disclosures at the times and in the sequence that the court orders. Absent a stipulation or court order, disclosures must be made (i) at least 90 days before the date set for trial or for the case to be ready for trial; or (ii) if intended solely to contradict or rebut another party's expert on the same subject matter, within 30 days after the other party's disclosure. Parties must supplement these disclosures when required under Rule 26(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Board practice, expert disclosure deadlines may be set differently (e.g., expert disclosure due 30 days before close of discovery). If a party wishes to rely on an expert after the deadline, it must file a motion for leave; late disclosure does not guarantee admission of testimony. Deadlines facilitate expert-related discovery and allow opposing parties to determine need for rebuttal experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Which experts must be disclosed and report obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties are not required to disclose consulting experts. Both retained, specially employed experts and unretained experts must be disclosed. Only retained experts are required to provide a written report unless otherwise stipulated; unretained experts must have subject matter and summary of facts/opinions disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2) distinctions. Determine whether an expert is 'retained' (enlistment for purpose of testimony) or an on-the-scene witness; retained experts typically trigger the report requirement. Parties should decide within the discovery period whether they will use experts because disclosure obligations and discovery timing may depend on that decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notifying the Board of expert disclosures and possible suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: Any party disclosing plans to use an expert must notify the Board that it has made the required disclosure (but should not file with the Board copies of the materials provided to adverse parties). The Board may then suspend proceedings to allow for discovery limited to experts; the suspension may leave, reset, or alter disclosure deadlines depending on circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice is to notify the Board concurrently with providing disclosures to the adversary. Notification facilitates discovery, but failure to notify the Board is not necessarily a ground to exclude testimony. The Board decides case-by-case whether to suspend unrelated activities and how to reset expert-related deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modification and waiver of disclosure obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure deadlines and obligations may be modified upon written stipulation of the parties approved by the Board, or upon a motion granted by the Board, or by order of the Board. Parties may agree to waive or otherwise modify their obligation to make disclosures, but must inform the Board by written stipulation or by motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a stipulation or motion for modification is denied, deadlines and obligations may remain as set or be reset; failure to make required or adequate disclosures may lead to motions to compel and sanctions, including possible judgment. In instances like defaults or certain motions, disclosure obligations may be stayed and later reset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and signature requirements for disclosures and discovery filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the court orders otherwise, all disclosures under Rule 26(a) must be in writing, signed, and served. Every disclosure under Rule 26(a)(1) or (a)(3) and every discovery request, response, or objection must be signed by at least one attorney of record (or the party if unrepresented) and must state the signer's address, e-mail address, and telephone number. By signing, an attorney or party certifies that to the best of their knowledge, after a reasonable inquiry: (A) a disclosure is complete and correct as of the time it is made; and (B) a discovery request/response/objection is consistent with the rules, warranted by existing law or nonfrivolous argument, not interposed for an improper purpose, and neither unreasonable nor unduly burdensome or expensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unsigned disclosures/requests/responses are subject to being struck until signed. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(g) for the certification obligations and consequences for violations. For discussions of duty to supplement and violations of Rule 26(g), see TBMP § 408.03 and § 408.01(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of discovery (relevance and admissibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may obtain discovery regarding any nonprivileged matter that is relevant to any party's claim or defense — including the existence, description, nature, custody, condition, and location of documents or other tangible things and the identity and location of persons who know of any discoverable matter. Relevant information need not be admissible at trial if the discovery appears reasonably calculated to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence. All discovery is subject to limits imposed by Rule 26(b)(2)(C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery may extend beyond matters specifically raised in the pleadings to any matter that might serve as the basis for additional claims or defenses, but fishing expeditions are prohibited. In TTAB proceedings the scope is often narrower than in district court, and proportionality principles apply (including with respect to ESI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to cooperate and proportionality in discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Each party has a duty to make a good faith effort to satisfy the discovery needs of its adversary and to make a good faith effort to seek only such discovery as is proper and relevant to the specific issues involved in the proceeding. Parties are expected to cooperate in the disclosure and discovery process and to discuss stipulations that may facilitate exchange of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board looks with extreme disfavor on parties who do not cooperate. Parties should discuss discovery conference topics set by Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f) and revisit discussions whenever expert witnesses become involved. Consider proportionality with regard to the needs of the case, prior discovery, amount in controversy, and importance of issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on discovery and Electronically Stored Information (ESI)
rubrics_metrics.description: A party need not provide discovery of ESI from sources that the party identifies as not reasonably accessible because of undue burden or cost. On a motion to compel or for protective order, the party resisting discovery must show that the information is not reasonably accessible; if shown, the requesting party must demonstrate good cause for production. The court/Board will consider whether the sought discovery is unreasonably cumulative or duplicative, obtainable from a more convenient source, whether the requesting party had ample opportunity to obtain it, and whether burden or expense outweighs likely benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the Board's limited jurisdiction and concern over excessive e-discovery, burden and expense of ESI production weigh heavily against requiring production in most TTAB cases. Parties should be precise in ESI requests and consider representative sampling or reduced productions where full compliance is unduly burdensome. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(2)(B) and related TBMP notes and case examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protections for privileged information and work product
rubrics_metrics.description: Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 exempts privileged information and work product from disclosure. Documents prepared in anticipation of litigation or for trial are discoverable only upon a showing that the requesting party has substantial need for the materials and cannot, without undue hardship, obtain the substantial equivalent by other means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidential commercial information discovery is subject to the Board's standard protective order or an appropriate alternative. Parties invoking privilege or work-product protection must be prepared to justify withholding; courts may order limited disclosure upon a showing of substantial need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative sampling as a remedy for undue burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Where complete compliance with a particular request for discovery would be unduly burdensome, the Board may permit the responding party to comply by providing a representative sampling of the information sought, or some other reduced amount of information sufficient to meet the propounding party's discovery needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative sampling is fact-specific. The Board's cases provide examples (e.g., representative invoices, limited sales figures, or production of a sample of documents) where full production would be unduly burdensome; in other situations full production may be required if not burdensome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failing to make initial disclosures and pretrial disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: A party that has not made initial disclosures may not serve discovery requests or file a motion for summary judgment, except for motions addressing the Board’s jurisdiction or claim/issue preclusion. Pretrial disclosures are not part of the disclosure and discovery process and a motion to compel is not the remedy when a party fails to make, or makes inadequate, pretrial disclosures. Parties are required to make pretrial disclosures prior to the opening of each testimony period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to make initial disclosures can preclude other procedural rights (e.g., serving discovery or moving for summary judgment) and may lead to motions to compel and sanctions. For details, see TBMP §§ 401, 702.01, and 411.01.
